extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of philosophy/history of science
extracted.subtask_description: A concise explanatory review of Thomas Kuhn's The Structure of Scientific Revolutions outlining the stages of disciplinary development, the dual senses of 'paradigm', the nature of normal science, anomalies and crises, and how paradigms are born and assimilated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-paradigmatic Stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a scientific discipline develops, there is normally a long period of somewhat inchoate, directionless research into a given subject matter with various competing schools offering fundamentally different conceptions of the basic problems and evaluation criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competing schools characterize this stage; there is no single set of accepted problems, methods, or standards. Research is fragmented and lacks a unified paradigm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergence of Normal Science
rubrics_metrics.description: Out of the competing schools one may emerge that subsequently dominates the discipline because its approach solves many problems and holds promise for future research; a particular outstanding achievement often causes the discipline to rally around that approach (a 'paradigm').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normal science follows from the community's rallying around a successful school; dominance arises from demonstrable problem-solving success and an exemplar achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms as Exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'paradigm' can mean the particular, concrete achievement that defines by example the course of all subsequent research (an 'exemplar') — e.g., Newton's mechanics, Franklin's theory of electricity, Copernicus' treatise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplars outline a unified approach to a wide-ranging set of problems; the problems, methods, theoretical principles, metaphysical assumptions, concepts, and evaluative standards that appear in such works constitute examples for subsequent research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms as Disciplinary Matrices
rubrics_metrics.description: Kuhn also uses 'paradigm' to refer to the entire cluster of problems, methods, theoretical principles, metaphysical assumptions, concepts, and evaluative standards present to some degree in an exemplar — a 'disciplinary matrix'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disciplinary matrix is the full theoretical, methodological, and evaluative framework within which scientists conduct research. Kuhn treats this sense as less fundamental than the exemplar sense because the exemplar effectively defines the matrix's elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific Community as Socially Defined Discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific discipline is defined socially: a particular scientific community united by education (texts, accreditation), professional interaction (journals, conventions), shared interests in problems, and acceptance of a particular range of possible solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership criteria, professional structures, and communication networks are integral; Kuhn leaves a detailed sociological definition to others but emphasizes the community's role in defining standards and what counts as science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of Exemplars in Education and Practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Exemplars are solutions to problems that serve as the basis for generalization and development; studying exemplars trains scientists to see new problems as similar and apply relevant principles rather than merely memorizing formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbooks often contain standard problems (e.g., pendulums, harmonic oscillators) used to teach application. Learning involves abstracting which problem features are relevant within the exemplar's theoretical framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal Science as Puzzle-Solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a paradigm is accepted, subsequent research consists of applying the shared methods of the disciplinary matrix to solve the types of problems defined by the exemplar; Kuhn characterizes this activity as 'puzzle-solving.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paradigm 'guarantees' that a solution exists for posed problems (though the precise solution/path may be unknown), so research focuses on solving well-defined puzzles within the framework rather than revising fundamentals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergence of Anomaly and Crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally problems persist and resist solution within the paradigm; if such anomalies persist, a sense of crisis can develop, leading some scientists to question fundamental assumptions and spawning competing conceptual schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anomalies congeal into differing schools of thought much like pre-paradigmatic competition. While many may still defend the old paradigm hoping it will resolve anomalies, widespread doubt about fundamentals may prepare the ground for change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Birth and Assimilation of a New Paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: A competing approach that produces a solution showing generality and promise may gain a loyal following and be regarded as a concrete achievement that functions as an exemplar; over time most scientists may switch loyalties and the new paradigm is assimilated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transition involves resistance (some persist or are marginalized), persuasion by growing success, and social dynamics (journals, positions). Learning a theory involves acquiring a new way of seeing—grouping problems differently—so assimilation requires cognitive as well as social shifts.
